**Sources read:**
- [EW] Enduring Word (David Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/
- [PC] Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- [EL] Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- [GI] Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm (the copy I got stops partway through v. 10)
- [PO] Matthew Poole: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm (the copy I got stops at v. 20)

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- Guzik reads "Jacob" as a pointed reminder of the name meaning "deceiver." Judah has the *name* Israel but not its character. Their ancestor Judah is no compliment either (Genesis 37–38). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/
- Pulpit: "Jacob" is the everyday name and "Israel" the covenant name. "Waters of Judah" narrows the address to the Jewish exiles. Swearing by the LORD shows they hadn't openly abandoned him, but it was only outward. Pulpit links this to Matthew 15:8, honouring God with the lips. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott: the phrase limits "Jacob/Israel" to the exiles from Judah. Their ideal titles are set against their real hypocrisy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Gill: they had "the name, not the thing." It was lip-worship, not worship "in spirit and truth." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 2:**
- Pulpit: boasting of the "holy city" shows they leaned on outward things, like "We are Abraham's seed" (John 8:33). They assumed the God of Israel was bound to protect them. "LORD of hosts" reminds them of his holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott hears irony here and compares Matthew 3:9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Gill: their trust was "feigned." He compares Micah 3:11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm
- Guzik: it was all image and no reality, and God saw through it. He quotes Motyer on Judah's "impeccable pedigree" that was all unreal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/

**v. 3:**
- Ellicott: this is the seventh time the prophet presses God's foreknowledge. This time it is aimed at Judah's "little faith" rather than the pagans' unbelief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Pulpit: the "former things" are contrasted with the "new things" of v. 6. It admits it is hard to say exactly which prophecies are meant and gives the views of Delitzsch and Kay. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Gill takes the "former things" as the promises to Abraham (Genesis 15:13): Egypt, the Exodus and Canaan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 4:**
- Pulpit: the word means hard or stiff, as in "stiff-necked." The neck is like a band of iron. The "brow of brass" may be where our word "brazen" comes from, and here it means defiance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Gill: they were shameless and unwilling to blush at sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm
- Ellicott: God foresaw both Cyrus's conquests and his own people's stubbornness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 5:**
- Pulpit: God made his prophecies more striking *because* Israel was stubborn. This was mercy, piling up evidence to win them, not punishment. It cites Ezekiel 20 as evidence of idolatry among the exiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Gill: God foretold things so they couldn't credit idols, as they had done with the golden calf. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm
- Guzik: Judah was left without excuse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/

**v. 6:**
- Pulpit: "Now see it all," meaning the prophecies fulfilled. Shouldn't they become God's witnesses (43:10)? Following Kay, it suggests the "new things" are Isaiah 49–53: Christ's coming and the new creation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott: the new things lie further off than Cyrus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Gill: the new things are Babylon's fall and Cyrus. These were pictures of redemption through Christ and the gospel, a "hidden mystery." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 7:**
- Pulpit: revealing what was hidden in God's counsel is "a sort of creation." It compares Ephesians 3:9. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott: "created" is an unusual verb for historical events. Things long in God's mind are now shown. God held them back because the people weren't ready (John 16:12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Gill: God makes no new decrees. "Created" means *revealed*, and he cites Kimchi for this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 8:**
- Pulpit: Israel had no "ears to hear." The verse returns to complaint. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Poole: the warnings were needed to cure their unbelief. "Called" a transgressor means they truly *were* one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm
- Gill and Guzik both read "from the womb" as including inborn sin (see section 2).

**v. 9:**
- Pulpit: having chosen Israel publicly, God was committed to protect it "for his Name's sake." Otherwise his name would be blasphemed among the nations (Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott sees two senses:
  - the nations would think God fickle if he destroyed his people;
  - "name" stands for his character, which is willing to save. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Gill: it was not for any merit of theirs. God held back his wrath so there would still be a people to praise him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm
- Guzik: mercy can never be deserved. God gives it for his own glory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/

**v. 10:**
- Pulpit and Ellicott: "not as silver" means less severe than refining silver, which is purified "seven times" (Psalm 12:6). Refining that hard would have destroyed Israel. "Chosen" is better translated "tested." Pulpit says the furnace is the Babylonian captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Poole: the aim is to purify, not consume. "In judgment I will remember mercy." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm
- Gill reviews several renderings and prefers "not among silver." If God kept them in the fire until all the dross was gone, they would be consumed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm
- Guzik: we are not the centre of the universe. Trials serve God's eternal purpose. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/

**v. 11:**
- Poole: "do it" means delivering them from Babylon. If God didn't, his name would be blasphemed, as if he were powerless or impossible to appease. He won't let idolaters take credit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm
- Pulpit: abandoning Israel would have handed his glory to a foreign god (cf. 42:8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott: "it" includes the whole work of redemption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 12:**
- Pulpit: "I am He" means the eternally unchanging One. It compares Romans 11:36. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott: this verse begins a condensed summary of chapters 40–47: God's oneness, eternity, power and knowledge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Poole: being "called" gives Israel the least excuse to follow idols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 13:**
- Pulpit: as Creator, God has a right to be obeyed. Everything in creation except man rises at once at his call. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Poole: "stand up" means either that they rose out of nothing at his command or that they stand ready to serve. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 14:**
- Pulpit: idol-worshippers are challenged again. "Him" is Cyrus, whom God "loved," just as Isaiah 45:1 calls him God's "anointed." The Hebrew of the last clause is "very harsh." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott: the verse could mean "He whom the LORD loves will do His pleasure," and it is probably *God's* pleasure. There may be a hint of David's name, which means "beloved." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Poole: God loved Cyrus with the general kindness he has for all creatures (Psalm 145:9), not with saving love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm
- Guzik takes the verse as a sign that God acts from love, not self-centredness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/

**v. 15:**
- Pulpit: God called Cyrus (46:11). Herodotus says Cyrus met no setback until his final campaign. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Poole: neither the foreknowledge nor the achievement can be credited to idols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 16:** Who "me" is gets debated; see section 2.

**v. 17:**
- Pulpit: God's teaching is for our benefit (2 Timothy 3:16), and so are the lessons of his providence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott: it speaks to people's wish for a "good investment." The Redeemer leads to the one lasting gain (Matthew 16:26). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Poole: if they fail to benefit, the fault is theirs, not God's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 18:**
- Pulpit and Ellicott: "the river" is literally the Euphrates. Pulpit compares Psalm 81:13–16 and Jesus' lament over Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Guzik: the verse shows potential left unused through disobedience. He quotes Redpath that just 24 hours of obedience would bring a "flood tide" of blessing from the Holy Spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/

**v. 19:**
- Pulpit: obedience would have fulfilled the promise to Abraham literally. Instead fewer than 50,000 returned (Ezra 2:64). The return was like a nation raised from the dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott: this is the sigh of every true teacher over what might have been (Luke 19:42). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Poole: their numbers were cut down because of sin (Numbers 14:34). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 20:**
- Pulpit: the command was needed because many exiles chose to stay. "Flee" means leaving corrupting company, not running from enemies. Following Kay, it calls the deliverance a prelude to the world's redemption. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott: act on God's promises and proclaim what he has done. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Guzik: the whole world should hear of God's mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/

**v. 21:**
- Pulpit says a literal miracle on the return journey "is not to be altogether excluded," though most commentators read the verse as symbolic. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott calls the literal reading "dead prosaic literalism." He takes water from the rock as a symbol of spiritual refreshment (John 4:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 22:**
- Pulpit and Guzik: the line returns as a refrain at 57:21. Guzik, citing Wolf, notes that both times it closes a nine-chapter section. Guzik links it to Psalm 73. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/
- Ellicott: even freedom and home are no blessing to the unworthy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Guzik: Isaiah 49 onward turns from Cyrus to the Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/

## 2. Where the readings differ

The pages don't state which tradition each writer belongs to, so I haven't added labels. These are differences between commentators, not denominational positions given by each tradition's own teachers.

**v. 16 (who is "me"?)**
- *The Messiah / God's Servant:* Guzik says the Messiah himself is speaking. He quotes Grogan, who notes that Young and Kidner hold this view. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/
- Pulpit reports Kay's view: one divine Person sent by another, the Son sent by the Father and the Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- *The prophet:* Pulpit rejects Kay, saying it goes against "the analogy of faith" for the Spirit to send the Son. It sides with Cheyne that the prophet is speaking, sent by the Father and the Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- Ellicott also says the prophet. He notes that some think of the Servant, and that some make the Spirit the one *sent* rather than the sender. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/48.htm
- Poole says Isaiah, but "a type of Christ." He reads "God and his Spirit" as God *by* his Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm

**v. 18 ("O that you had listened"): how can God "wish"?**
- Poole: God's wishes shouldn't be taken literally, as if he longed for something he couldn't bring about. They express what he approves and commands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm
- Guzik and Redpath stress blessing missed through disobedience, without discussing that question. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/

**v. 8 ("rebel from birth")**
- Gill and Guzik apply it to inborn sin in every person. Guzik cites Romans 5:12, sin inherited from Adam. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-48/
- Gill applies it even to "God's elect." He reads the "birth" mainly as Israel's birth as a nation in the Exodus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm
- Pulpit and Poole don't make the original-sin point. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm

## 3. Other views (only partly found)

**Older text and translation notes:**
- v. 10: Gill notes that the Septuagint, Vulgate and Syriac read "furnace of poverty." He rejects changing the text to "as silver." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/48.htm
- v. 14: Pulpit says the Hebrew "perhaps requires emendation." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- v. 18: Pulpit rejects Cheyne's rendering of "righteousness" as "prosperity." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-48.html
- v. 18: Poole, unlike Pulpit, does take it as peace and prosperity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/48.htm

**Not found:**
- the Wesleyan, Lutheran or Pentecostal sites
- netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes
- Catholic or Orthodox readings
- any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter

Gill on vv. 10–22 and Poole on vv. 20–22 were also cut off. When the tool is available again, the most useful next steps are:
- netbible.org notes on v. 16
- church fathers on v. 16 at newadvent.org
- wesley.nnu.edu on v. 18
- Spurgeon (spurgeon.org) on the "furnace of affliction" in v. 10
